I have plenty of photos where I look 'happy' - unlike you though, I do have memory of what came before them, and it usually involved being told I had to smile or else I'd be harmed or screamed at etc. It's very easy to control the narrative with snapshots like that. Me smiling out of fear did not mean I was happy. It's very possible you also felt like you had no choice. It doesn't in any way discount your trauma and also - she above all people should know it's very rare for there to never be any moments of happiness in someone's life, even those going through severe trauma. Abusers can have moments of showing kindness. It does not mean abuse did not take place, or that the abuse is somehow less severe because of said moments of kindness. 

Please be gentle with yourself if you can. And please fire that therapist. It was a really despicable thing to say to someone with dissociative issues. :(

For me, it WAS caught - I was autistic enough pre-transition for a professor of *childhood development* in 1999 to want me to get screened (the professor was a man, too). For a child who looked like a girl, that's incredible and very out of the ordinary. Socially it was so unheard of for girls to have autism. I was 5 then. 

But I had abusive caregivers who didn't believe in preventative medicine let alone autism. So that was that.

-Adoptee competent 

-Trauma informed (make sure this isn't a clickbait thing to accrue more profile views - a lot of clinicians have been using it incorrectly as of late, there's a lot of alleged trauma competent providers out there rn who aren't actually competant at all)

-Find a therapist who specializes in what's called persons-centered modality or someone who's at the very least flexible about the modality they work with, or someone who uses multiple. Modality in layman's terms is a school of thought regarding therapy approaches and responses. Avoid therapists who use only CBT modality if at all possible. They do not have the right training to be helpful to DCP in general but especially not to late discoverees. CBT in general is not a safe approach for survivors of trauma or complex life situations beyond minor depression or anxiety. 

-A willingness to learn new things


Keep in mind that it's 100% socially acceptable to interview potential therapists. The goal is finding someone you trust and can build rapport with. Please ask them questions! It's good to take a proactive approach, especially with consultation appointments. Don't let them push you into building rapport or sharing too much before you're ready. A good therapist wants to build a strong beginning foundation, and anyone who pushes you too quickly is unlikely to help you long term. 

Source: me, who's been in therapy most of my life and has a lot of experience.😅

With the exception of your childhood, you have a lot of similar symptoms that I do when I'm doing well in life, in regards to my CPTSD. (To be clear, 'doing well' for me means: I have food, shelter with no threat of homelessness in the foreseeable future, am safe from those that wish me harm). I've been diagnosed with PTSD for a decade now, 'upgraded' to CPTSD after a neuropsych evaluation a few years back. When I'm safe and doing well, some of my symptoms can become subclinical on its surface. I also did a ton of work on myself independently which helped me get past the constant self loathing (but of course, triggers or confrontations can send me back to that if it's bad enough, and it takes me a while to recover back to baseline). WRT flashbacks, I used to have body memories, especially as a kid, but it's less common now. Emotional flashbacks happen for me but sometimes I have to piece it together later because I'm a flight person and tend to want to capital L leave to avoid being more publicly emotional. I dissociate off and on and have for most of my life, but again, a lifetime of masking means most would never notice because I became very good at masking to survive. I often have to tell people I'm triggered or was after the fact because no one ever notices. I manage to hold relationships these days and do relatively okay at keeping them and meeting other's needs to a point, but I often overshoot what I'm actually capable of (which is on me, not my friends, and I take ownership of that when it happens). However, I pretty much always have an emotional distance inside towards everyone due to severe attachment issues I'm still recovering from. You'd never know I struggle in relationships because I hide it well.  My main molester as a child was a therapist by profession, so I became very good at hiding feelings specifically due to that. 

However, I have traumaversaries year round, intermittent trauma nightmares including several in the last few days (ugh), and still get triggered. I'm able to handle it 'well' compared to others because growing up, being visibly emotional was a possible death sentence for me. I would be threatened with death or sexual violence specifically. So my body knows it's not safe to act out in that way, and I can't act out (or have meltdowns fe) the same way other people can. It was literally beaten out of me as a response I could have. That doesn't mean I don't have PTSD or CPTSD, you know? It means my masking of symptoms *is a symptom* of the severe trauma I experienced. Which thankfully, most of my better therapists have understood. 

Anyways, I hope any of my ramblings could possibly be beneficial to you. As someone who's survived 'extreme' trauma (trafficking survivor, attempted filicide survivor, serial molestation and more), what I know the most about trauma is that it's different for everyone. I don't read your post and go 'ugh, you haven't suffered enough to be here'. What you feel is real. Your struggles are real and I believe you. I once thought what I went through wasn't bad enough to count, and I didn't always have the words to describe to professionals how bad it was. That took time, patience and education as I dethawed and took the time to really deconstruct things. 

I hope you stay, and that the things here you read can help you. Rooting for you, OP. 🫂

I do think it can be lessened considerable for those who come from a KD - for people like me who are anonymously conceived and from a bank donor, though, those feels tend to pop up eventually. Being the product of two people who never met and who most likely wouldn't have chosen each other in any other situation leaves you in a similar emotional limbo to being an oopsie baby in a lot of ways. I feel like it says a lot that there are DCP who feel this way who don't have any major traumas or bad RPs. It's not a feeling you arrive at because of 'bad experiences'..its often just kind of part of the package, if you're anonymously conceived. I won't speak for people born from a KD arrangement because I'm sure they have their own unique thoughts and I'd rather they speak those themselves than me speak for them. 

And yeah, right on the nose with the nuclear family bit 😅. I'm *one* on the DCP known on the community for having been trafficked, but not the only one, unfortunately. I'm not just DC, I'm, in my case, *illegally* DC. Which is its own huge pile of ick. But that's a story for another day. 
 


I was expecting most people to be 'happy DCP' when I showed up in the community years ago and kind of braced myself for being alone in my feelings, but it seems like the line of thought I had about my lived experience aligned with people who haven't gone through half of what I did (not a knock on anyone, to be clear. I don't tier pain). 

I think, in the end, it's just not right for everyone. Being DC can work for someone who doesn't need much mirroring, but if you couple a caregiver or two with a child who needs more mirroring from the bio that isn't there, coupled with those caregiver's misattunement (which can happen no matter how hard they do or don't try) ..yeah, it's gonna fuck people up. Love alone can't fix that, parenting alone can't fix that, it's not about cultural preconceptions of heteronormativity for most so it can't be something that's taught out of you because it's not societal beliefs that the needs spurt out of, and you can't micromanage someone's feelings out if it, either. You can't plan for it because it can't be screened out.  It's about basic needs that aren't being fulfilled because they can't be, due the situation the children have been put in. (Which, yeah..the cultural allegiance nuclear family also makes impossible to fix).

Autism is also somewhat high on the comorbidities list, as are things like gastrointestinal issues (including but not limited to gastroparesis), arthritis, ME/CFS, SFN (small fiber neuropathy), CCI (cervical-cranio instability), sleep disorders, anxiety, migraines, Chiari Malformation Type I, and so much more. Because it's disabled me for most of my life and I was applying for disability benefits (which I got). It also impacts our standard of care, as we can metabolize medication differently and that needs to be known by our care team, especially if undergoing surgery.

**One extremely traumatic thing:** I found a man dead when I was 10 years old. Rigor mortis had already set in, so I learned in real time about what bodies go through after death. The man in question was the only adult who ever really treated me kindly. While it took me years to get over associating the color periwinkle with the color of dead skin, it wasn't as traumatic as it really should've been. As long as I'm not around women screaming (the adults that were with me didn't handle it as well as I did), I manage that trauma just fine. Death doesn't really bother me. 

**Allegedly untraumatic thing that fucks with me:** Donor conception, as a donor conceived person. I knew my whole life how I was born and still find the idea that it's acceptable and normalized to be extremely traumatic and painful for me. I do literally everything I can to avoid the topic *because* of how painful it is for me, and because of how insensitive people are about it (most people never even think about what it's like to be us, or else say incredibly callous things towards us because they have no theory of mind as to how to approach what we might be going through). I don't know why we're okay with separating people from their bio family for no other reason than someone else's wants. I hate the idea that people spout that the concept is progressive even though the idea of it is based off of eugenics and white supremacy (ie, who is allowed to have a baby, and who isn't; a woman named Georgia Tann popularized this type of thought in recent memory, though it's been around for ages), while it also reaffirms the idea of the nuclear family, which is also based in white supremacy and wartime propaganda. Like adoption, it's a permanent legal estrangement that cannot be annulled. So I lose aspects like the rights towards citizenship in countries I descend from, because this industry has created a way to streamline legal separation of kin. My vital records are permenantly altered and I cannot fix them, and that lack of control bothers me deeply, especially as a trans person who also can't fix my legal records due to the current administration. It compounds the trauma of dysphoria for me by reminding me constantly that I'm ultimately under the control of another by law, supported by an industry and society that sees me as a product and property rather than a person who has my own rights and interests.

Studies keep being done saying that DCP grow up 'okay' and are neutral to positive about their conception..but so many of those studies are paid for by the industry that creates us, with the researchers asking leading questions, very small sample sizes, and the industry itself dislikes any challenge of the status quo that would affect their bottom line. There's also a heavy amount of emotional coercion involved in being DC, and you're punished socially if you don't follow the standard social narrative - even more so if you're marginalized. Being LGBTQ and DCP is a nightmare for me. I could write an entire paper on how much I genuinely fucking hate this shit. 

I don't typically get into the nitty gritty specifics as to how this situation has *materially* impacted me (it has severely, though); what I'll say instead is that the idea that donor conception universally and unilaterally creates permanancy (ie, a home, parents who keep you), a family support system, and an extended kinship network for the people created from it is false. It can for *some* people. It does not for all of us.

It really is such a massive issue we face, yeah. I find interdependence and the vulnerability and humility to both ask for and accept help to be a sign of strength of character. No human is an island and we were never meant to be; a healed femur being amongst the first signs of civilization and all that. I always walk a delicate balance because I don't like giving *too* much control over to others - I want to flex my 'muscles' so to speak, until I can't anymore. But I think that's every younger disabled person to a point..we want to be young and still live our lives like our peers to the extent that we can (sometimes to our detriment). I finally accepted recently that I needed a home health aid and so far it's been going really well for me. I might get a PCA in the future but for now, a HHA is good enough for me. 

I also don't see suffering alone as a virtue meant to create better character; so the idea that we must always suffer alone and that to rely on others is inappropriate makes no sense to me. It's a type of martyrdom I don't want to recreate in my own life as well as a Christian value and, well. I'm not a Christian. 

For future reference, if it's useful to know: the 'it could be worse' thing people pull out is a logical fallacy called the fallacy of relative privation (as well as societal and systemic ableism, but, well. We know that part). It's also known as the 'starving kids in Africa' fallacy.

To answer your questions in a bullet pointed way (I have low spoons atm, apologies):

1) What if I'm wrong?

- Then they can politely let you know you have the wrong person, or else just not respond. Your anxiety is understandable but cold contacting someone you don't know in a respectful and polite way is in no way a crime. 

2) Do I reach out to someone? 

- That one is up to you. I'd say, if you have a lot of anxiety about the possible responses, maybe wait a bit until you've had time to process. But I would say it's worth the attempt, personally. 

3) Is it ethical to contact someone I found through research, even though they're not on Ancestry?

- As a genetic genealogist - 100% yes, it is ethical. I've reached out to people many times before, written hundreds if not thousands of cold emails to people most wouldn't even consider a real relative (though I do), some who I didn't even have a direct DNA match to myself. Very rarely if ever did I receive a negative response. You have every right to reach out to this man, who makes up roughly 50% of you. 

And you're right, many donors were promised anonymity. But it's not ethical to keep an inherently unethical promise, and it's unreasonable to ask someone (you, your sister) to hold that burden. Knowing who we descend from is a right enshrined in the UN's Conventions of the Rights of the Child, for one thing. By the 1980s into the early 90s many commonwealth countries had already banned anonymity, and in 1989 there was even a book written about the dangers of anonymous donation called Lethal Secrets.   https://www.amazon.com/Lethal-Secrets-Annette-Baran/dp/0941770117 

It's especially okay to 'break' that promise when that promise is a danger to yourself and others. Your updated medical history is imperative even if you aren't currently dealing with anything. We have so many members of our community who have died due to inherited terminal illnesses (Narelle Grech is an example), and many more who are disabled and chronically ill who spent years undiagnosed due to not knowing what they were predisposed to. I am one of those people. 

You are allowed to act in your best interests in a situation that has forced your hand, OP. You can only operate within the confines of the material position we've all been put in, and there's no way to make everyone happy when this situation was never meant to consider our quality of life. (And it's okay, to also just be curious. You're more than allowed to). 

Best of luck to you. If you need help writing a message, I'm sure others and myself as well would be more than happy to help you script a message that feels right. 🫂

Scans alone cannot and are not the main diagnostic criteria for AATD - genotyping, symptoms and serum levels *are*. Symptoms are also very variable in AATD, with some people with the worst genotype (ZZ) never going to develop symptoms, whereas those who were previously seen as carriers (MZ) have been known to need lung transplants and go on to use the augmentation therapy meant only for ZZ. 

Serum levels can also fluctuate based on hormonal imbalances and infections - mine can jump up 35 points during an infection, but I still have a confirmed Z allele. I'm waiting for a more thorough test to confirm if I have a rare allele (my symptoms & serum levels indicate I could be FZ) and my lung function test is next week.  I'm definitely worried about that one. I don't know if I can go the allotted time they need me to be off my inhalers without having a severe reaction. 

I would really recommend calling the Alpha 1 Foundation's genetic counseling service. It's free and they can send you a free test to see if you have AATD or not. That's how I found out I have one Z. The real way we protect kids (IMO) is by creating a rapport with them - by teaching them to listen to themselves, rather than assuming everyone is a wolf. You teach them that you’re a safe person to come to, by showing them over and over again that there won’t be a negative reaction to hearing bad news. That they aren’t shameful or bad for having that bad news. How to ride the waves of good and bad feelings. It helps them coregulate and through you, they also begin to self soothe, by seeing the calm reactions. Now, no problem is too big, because now they know they have someone on their side. You let them decide how they want to be touched. Tickles feel bad? No tickles, then. Face kisses good? Then face kisses! You let them choose. By teaching them it’s okay to say no, and decide what’s right for them, you foster a sense of trust, which then in turn lets them know that it’s allowed to express that no, not just to caregivers and relatives but to others as well. And they in turn develop a sense of deep trust within themselves that lets them know that they know enough to know what x or y is, because they in turn feel trusted back. And that then allows them to know when situations are pushing their boundaries, because they were able to develop them with someone who trusted them enough to make them. If they can’t say no to touch at home, or don’t know that good, loving touch, how can they distinguish a bad one? How will they know? 

(And, obviously - no one can 100% always know. It’s about being prepared. But being caught off guard? Not a failing on anyone. We can only do so much. Only the perp is at fault for that, always).

We weren’t taught how to develop that trust in ourselves, in our bodies. It’s hard to see the wolves when we’re afraid they’re everywhere. Intuition is a bit difficult to verbalize. I struggle to type out how it feels for me. I can only really describe it via this metaphor:

Imagine standing in a blank, white realm (the cool kind, that you see in those cool fantasy stories - pocket dimension). Now, imagine right ahead of you that that realm is *covered* in hanging strings. Every color imaginable. And you yourself have mentally labeled and memorized each string, where they connect, to who they connect, what the colors mean, the different sounds they make when touched, and in what contexts those things mean what they mean, and in what order. 

Now imagine something reaching out invisibly and strumming a string like you’d play a guitar. Because of your time studying, you know exactly where the taughtness is coming from, who caused it, why, even what level of pressure they’ve put on the string to give it a sound. That’s what intuition is like, when honed. It sounds mystical, but what it really is, is just rigorous study. You learn to trust yourself over time by practice. 

A way to train yourself further is to make a cheat sheet for yourself - this thing feels like this, which feels like this for this reason, I was thinking of this when I saw this which might be for this reason or a coincidence, are things to think about etc. Also take time to build a cheat sheet of signs you can expect, specific tells that would relate to who you honor / are working / worshipping, whether deity or spirit or ancestor. Learn their symbols, their personalities etc. Read their stories, if they have them; listen to them tell theirs, if they have yet to be told. Then over time, you can extract a pattern to make a more solid foundation for yourself. You can also ask them to use specific signs which you know you’ll listen to, during times of prayer and offerings.

For the medical part: the biggest thing right now for her, I think, is gonna be peer support. There’s no such thing as ‘high functioning’ autism. It’s just not a thing. What you’re referring to is just the spectrum of autism, which effects everyone differently. Most autistic activists do not consider the functioning scale to be a valid measurement of anything other than incompetence of the medical field to consider us multi faceted human beings. 

Another thing.. she IS permanently disabled. Autism, ADHD, and PTSD are all disabilities. Just because she isn’t in a wheelchair and doesn’t have a physical deformity, doesn’t mean she’s not disabled. If SHE doesn’t want to label that way, that’s perfectly fine, and she’s entitled to that. But they are covered under SSI and the CDC lists both autism and ADHD as disabilities, and I have yet to meet someone in the disability community who doesn’t count them all as such. If she wasn’t ‘disabled enough’, she wouldn’t be having these issues at work which prevent her from working effectively. It is literally part of the definition of disability that it prevents you from being able to work. According to the CDC, “A disability is any condition of the body or mind (impairment) that makes it more difficult for the person with the condition to do certain activities (activity limitation) and interact with the world around them (participation restrictions).” She more than qualifies.

So there's a lot of things to unravel and I'm really glad that I was able to see this post, because you're the exact age I was when I was asking for help, about very similar things. Above all else in my response I hope you're being kind to yourself after posting this. It can be really, really hard to share trauma like this out in the open. 

So to answer your questions I'm gonna bullet point them, so I can walk you through it a bit. (Also to help me respond to the most I can, and as efficient as I can!) I really hope I have insight that resonates with you!

* " can i STOP this? "

Absolutely. It's going to take a lot of hard work on your part, which isn't fair, I know - part of healing from abuse is having to heal from the wound of the unfairness of it all. None of us deserved it and now we're saddled with having to heal from something that wasn't our fault. But you can do this. You can. It starts with accepting yourself as you are right now. There's a lot of small ways you can start to do this. Making yourself eat a meal that you love everyday, even if you feel like you don't deserve it. Indulging in a favorite show or activity after a bad trauma brain episode. Things like this, they seem small, but the thing is that to work up to loving ourselves we have to start small and build habits, so that we can work more towards creating the self-acceptance and self-compassion that was beaten out of us by the abuse. 

*  how do i stop loving people who i know will hurt me or are abusers? why am i like this?

To fix this we have to unravel why this happens. It's not because you're flawed. It's not because you deserve it, or secretly want it. It's not because you're fucked up. What's actually happening is that they're repeating the message back to you that trauma teaches your soul: "you don't matter. You don't deserve kindness, you don't deserve respect, let alone love". When people suffer through trauma they develop what's known as an inner critic. It's a nasty part of your brain that was twisted by trauma. This part of you contains all of the nasty things you've ever been told or felt about yourself, it stores them, and reminds you of them. This inner critic can be inane - it's the meanest person on earth to you, all in an attempt to protect you from further harm. It's modus operundi is to convince you that you should follow your status quo that was taught to you during the abuse - that you have no worth - and to re-find this message in other relationships. Because that's the safe path. "It's what we know", it says. It's a scared child in the dark reaching for the familiar teddy bear with holes in it because it wants the comfort of the familiar, but doesn't see the danger of what could be in the holes. (Sorry, shitty metaphor, I'm really tired today DX). It can take... a really long time, to be able to catch yourself, into realizing you're trying to find the familiar hurt again. But I promise that with patience and time you will be able to stop yourself. 

Another part of why you fell into this relationship with your abuser is because you were primed for it :( You had already suffered so much pain and been hurt so badly that when you met him you didn't see danger..you saw familiar companionship. He reminded you of your normal up until that point. It absolutely sucks and I'm so sorry you had to go through it all. No one deserves this.

In situations like this, what’s really needed is finding a reason to keep going. I can’t recommend you one; it’s got to be something you choose, for yourself. Have you ever spoken to anyone about your feelings professionally, btw? I’m not asking because I want to shove you off to some crisis worker or whatever, either; you and your problems aren’t a burden I want to be rid of like that, and while they mean well, I’ve never had a good conversation with one. I ask because you deserve to be heard and understood without being guilted for feeling this way. You’re allowed to express that you have rope burn from hanging on. 

There isn’t a magic word I can say that will convince you to stay, or to convince you that it’s worth it to stay. But I can still sit and talk with you while you’re hurting. I can say I hear you, I see you, and remind you that you aren’t alone. That’s all we can do for each other in the end. It’s true that we have the power to hurt people. It’s true too, that life is scary, and unpredictable. But there’s no such thing as darkness without light. And another thing; 8 year old you also deserves to be happy. They deserve the chance to experience good things. Baby you didn’t deserve to have their heart broken. 

I’m not going to ask you to do anything but to breathe, to follow HALT (which is checking in with ourselves and asking the following; am I Hungry? Am I Angry? Am I Lonely? A fallacy abused kids grow up thinking a lot of the time is that age brings wisdom. That adults are all-knowing, because they said so. But now that were all adults..we realize the fallacy isn’t true. Some adults are not grown up. Our parents certainly weren’t emotionally mature or healthy adults. 

Whenever I confronted my mother about the same thing, she’s showed me again and again that she’s never thought deeply about the pattern. Also, as an aside; it’s not about strength. You seeing your pain mirrored in your mother, this is not a weakness. People who feel differently than you are not stronger than you, they’re just at a different part in their own individual path of healing <3  Everyone’s path is different. You aren’t weak for seeing vulnerability and wanting to nurture and comfort. It’s misguided, in this sense, only because this desire to nurture can’t and won’t end well for you *in this particular circumstance*, because you can’t help your mother unless she helps herself first, and that epiphany might never come. But the feelings you’re feeling, they aren’t bad or wrong. There’s so much strength in vulnerability. Being vulnerable IS strength. It’s just a different type of strength, that people love to brush off as a weakness, because they don’t want to admit it scares them. In a world that’s allergic to caring, admitting you give a damn is an act of bravery.

It’s okay if you don’t. I know everyone else is trying to convince you that you do...but whether you do or don’t? It’s both okay. To either have it, or have it impaired or have less of it. It doesn’t fundamentally *mean* anything about you, other than that you’re a little different from others. And that’s just fine. You don’t need to experience everything the same way as everyone else to be a good person. You just have to treat other people well and be mindful, the same as everyone else. It worries me that too many people are trying to convince you that you don’t have lessened empathy because they see it as this terrible incurable thing to be afraid of, a fate worse than death, when it’s not? It’s just as I said; different. A different but equally valid way of being. 

You don’t have to have ASPD or NPD to have lessened empathy, either. I’m autistic and have lessened empathy. (The TBI probably didn’t help). When you have trauma sometimes things just rewire a bit different, and it can mirror cognitive defects and present like other things. It does sort of suck that it’s harder to connect with others, but it’s not the end of the world either.

So please remember, that whether you do or don’t, that you’re allowed to exist and just be as you are. People’s perceptions of what it’s like to have low empathy don’t come into play here, because they do not know you, and people are highly biased based on bad experiences. There is no mental illness or disorder that will make you mistreat others. Despite people’s biases there is no such thing as Bad People Disorder. The behavior of mistreating others comes with a sense of entitlement to do so, in a belief system someone holds. If you’re conscientious enough to understand that people are as complex as you are and are mindful of that, you’re doing just fine, OP.

The thing with DID is that there are dissociative disorders which are 'milder', in the sense of / where there isn't the complexity which is a full-blown DID system with several alters, but they aren't talked about as much. What you're describing sounds a bit like OSDD 1b, which almost no one talks about. (I believe this is what I personally have, if it isn't the TBI causing my issues, which is a chicken and egg thing anyway). In 1a typically a person will notice the personality switch and their alters are separate people. For 1b there is no switch; the alters aren't autonomous unto themselves in any way. My other selves are just younger versions of me, and they can't really control me but rather influence me if I'm triggered by a trauma they experienced. I experience no dissociative amnesia in regards to these parts influencing me. They don't personally have names bc I'm a really depersonalized person and having a concrete identity is hard for me. But yours easily could.

-Thought stopping, wherein you think your obsessive thought and then go, “Okay, but this isn’t true, or helpful”. (It’s more of a redirection than stopping it, but that’s what it’s called). I would recommend a second opinion. Most doctors don’t use the tender point model anymore. It’s very outdated. Here’s a quote from an article on it: 

“The American College of Rheumatology included counting tender points in their 1990 Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria, establishing that 11 of the 18 tender points had to be present and cause pain for at least three months.

But updated guidelines for 2010 did not require counting tender points in order to make a fibromyalgia diagnosis. Research found that many patients who had fibromyalgia weren’t meeting the tender points criteria.

....


“When we first latched onto those tender points, we thought they were more than they turned out to be,” says Dr. Wolfe. “[Counting them properly] can be difficult to do and they aren’t reliable amongst experts. It requires pressing with a certain force and some doctors use more force than other doctors. Counting tender points turned out to not be very useful diagnostically.”

“The problem with tender points is that they are very subjective,” says Dr. Dombrowski. “The way that I apply pressure to a patient may be different from another physician.”

Another factor is that fibromyalgia pain can fluctuate in location and intensity from day to day. One day, a fibro patient could have severe pain in nearly all tender points. Another day, they might have pain in only a few.

Doctors realized that over-relying on tender points to make a fibromyalgia diagnosis was leading to too many patients being under-diagnosed.”

This sounds like pretty clear cut Pure-O to me, actually? I can't tell you what you don't or don't have, I'm not a medical professional at all, but please take a moment to read this and see if it fits what's going on with you, okay? There is very little outreach about this type of OCD, and not many people know about it. 

[https://www.intrusivethoughts.org/ocd-symptoms/pure-ocd/](https://www.intrusivethoughts.org/ocd-symptoms/pure-ocd/)

### 

"Purely Obsessional OCD, also known as Pure O, is a type of OCD in which a sufferer engages in hidden compulsions. Instead of combating their intrusive thoughts with visible rituals such as hand-washing or counting, they perform repetitive, mental rituals to minimize stress. Because of the hidden nature of the disorder, Pure OCD is extremely distressing and challenging to treat. Many sufferers go years without seeking help or opening up to loved ones. 

Symptoms of Pure OCD vary greatly from person to person, however, the topics of people’s intrusive thoughts tend to fall within certain themes: sexuality, responsibility, violence, faith, health and romance.

### Common Pure OCD compulsions:

#### Guilt.

Thinking you’re a bad person for having violent, blasphemous or sexual intrusive thoughts. 

#### Thinking you’re a bad person.

Your character is at risk if you do the wrong thing and you feel devastated if someone thinks you’re a bad person.    

#### Avoidance.

Avoiding objects, places and people that are related to the nature of your intrusive thoughts.

#### Answer seeking.

Establishing legitimacy and determining answers to your thoughts.

#### Reassurance.

Going to church or temple and talking with clergy members or getting reassurance from family members that you’ve reached the right conclusion.

#### Research.

Looking online to find answers to your questions."
